title: Antifreeze proteins in action: structural determinants, hydration dynamics, and ice-binding mechanisms
content: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) constitute a broad class of biological macromolecules that extend the lifespan of various organisms, including bacteria, fungi, algae, diatoms, plants, insects, and fish, by inhibiting ice growth under extreme icy conditions. We discuss the molecular mechanisms behind the specificity of AFPs in recognizing a particular water polymorph, “ice”, preventing recrystallization and regulating ice growth, emphasizing their irreversible adsorption onto ice. Various structural motifs, ice-recognition mechanisms underlying antifreeze activity, and factors that enhance their antifreeze function are explained. In synergy with experimental structural biology techniques, advanced computational methods have played an essential role in elucidating the correlations among structure, protein hydration dynamics, and the functions of different classes of AFPs. In particular, advances in water-model development, improvements in sampling techniques, and free-energy calculations enable us to elucidate the origin of the unusual hydration dynamics of this group of proteins, which are crucial for ice recognition. This review discusses how molecular modeling and advanced molecular dynamics simulations shape our understanding of key aspects of AFP-mediated inhibition of ice growth. The findings presented herein can form the basis for designing AFP-inspired materials and their synthetic mimetics to regulate ice formation, which possess immense potential in the cryopreservation of biological cells, tissues, and different organs; the storage and delivery of perishable foods; the freeze-thaw degradation of cement-based substances; and the advancement of surfaces designed to prevent ice accumulation for aerospace vehicle, solar panel, and wind applications.
